title: DFS in Mumbai: Find a Path, Go Deep!
description: Watch DFS dive through a real street-map graph, exploring routes by going as deep as possible before backtracking. This visualization shows how depth-first search systematically reaches targets using only local decisions and a visited set.
ig_caption:
🌿🚦 **DFS in Bandra West (Mumbai)** — exploring the map by going *deep* first! 

🧠 **How DFS works (in graph terms):** Depth-First Search (DFS) treats the street network as a **graph** where intersections are **nodes** and roads are **edges**. Starting from a source node, DFS repeatedly chooses an unvisited neighbor, pushing the exploration forward like a stack—then **backtracks** when it hits a dead end. ✅ The **visited set** prevents cycles, ensuring we don’t wander in circles forever. 

🗺️ **On real street maps:** Even real-world road data becomes a sparse graph, so DFS’s behavior is heavily shaped by **neighbor ordering**—change the expansion order, and the traversal path can differ while still remaining complete (for a connected component). 

📌 Want to see **BFS vs DFS vs Dijkstra** on the same Mumbai map next? Comment your pick 👇 and follow for more pathfinding visuals! ✨
fb_caption:
🧩 **Pathfinding with DFS in Mumbai (Bandra West)**! 

Depth-First Search (DFS) is a fundamental graph search technique: it explores a route by going as far as possible along each branch before backtracking. Using a **street-map graph** (intersections = nodes, roads = edges), DFS relies on a **stack-like traversal** plus a **visited set** to avoid revisiting nodes and getting stuck in loops.
